To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the spatial mismatch between FDG‐PET and intracranially recorded epileptiform activity suggests that extending the intracranial coverage at least 1 cm beyond the hypometabolic cortex would increase the sensitivity of SOZ localization by FDG‐PET.

the spatial mismatch between the metabolic and EEG epileptic abnormalities in children with epilepsy undergoing intracranial EEG evaluation is at least 3 cm and that the spatial relationship is better in children with a smaller SOZ.

SPM utilizing pseudocontrols can reliably identify the lobe of the seizure onset zone, but the spatial mismatch with the intracranial EEG epileptiform changes suggests that the extent of the seizure onset area could be more precisely defined by expanding the coverage of intracranially recorded EEG at least by 3 cm.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods for the analysis of 3D surface data.
the study of the spatial relationship between FDG‐PET and ECoG‐determined SOZ in children with intractible epilepsy undergoing two‐stage surgery.

the development and validation of an innovative method for the detection of epileptogenic zones in patients with drug‐resistant focal epilepsy using a combined approach of statistical parametric mapping of FDG‐pet and intracranially recorded electrocorticograms (ECoG).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the spatial resolution of FDG‐SPM is insufficient to reliably detect the extent of the SOZ in pediatric focal epilepsies.

SPM utilizing pseudo‐controls could reliably detect the lobar level of the SOZ, but the mismatch between metabolic and ECoG‐EEG abnormalities indicates the need for extending the coverage of intracranical electrode beyond the metabolic abnormal region at least 3 cm.
the spatial resolution of FDG‐SPECT is not good enough to be used as an independent diagnostic tool.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a novel methodology for the evaluation of the spatial relationship between FDG‐PET hypometabolism and intracranially recorded epileptiform abnormalities.

we were able to show that FDG‐PET is a reliable tool for localizing the lobe of epilepsy origin in children, however the spatial mismatch between the FDG‐PET and EEG‐defined SOZ indicates that the extent of electrode coverage should be at least 3cm beyond the metabolic abnormal area.
we have shown that the spatial mismatch between the metabolic abnormality and the seizure onset zone is significant.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the spatial mismatch between FDG‐PET and intracranially recorded EEG abnormalities indicates that a full coverage of the SOZ by intracranial EEG electrodes may not be feasible with current electrode coverage.

the extent of intracranially detected seizure onset zone (the region of brain where seizure starts and propagates) may be underestimated by FDG‐PET alone and may extend beyond the region of hypometabolism.

the extent of intracranially recorded epileptiform abnormalities (interictal spikes and ictal onset zones) exceeds the extent of the hypometabolic cortex in the vast majority of children with epilepsy undergoing epilepsy surgery.
